Enclosure

October 1, 2026

This was quite the project. My back hurts.

For the project, I wanted to lay it all on line in terms of getting a successful version working by class time. As usual, I got kinda close.

The goal here was to make an enclosure for my headphones while maintaining an Art Deco theme. I took inspiration from the Bullcock Wilshire Building in Los Angeles and directly copied it's grille for my headphones case. I also specifically wanted to use teal or turquoise acrylic as many Art Deco buildings specifically use this color in their glazed terracotta façades.

I also wanted to use two materials here and both engrave and cut on the laser machine. So, I decided to make fairly intricate walls of the case with cut acrylic and used wood for my lid. The base was an engraved acrylic.

As usual, before started, I mocked everything up in Blender using AI. The blender looked amazing after working with it for a while, and I figured it was worth it to spend more on acrylic given how much effort I was going to put in. After going to Canal Plastics, I got an 18x32in sheet of acrylic, which gave me lots of room to fail.

I then started to laser cut. I started with the wall, which I split up into two laser cuts: the cut for the left/right/front and the cut for the back. The longer cut was to be best bended around a jig and placed atop the bottom. I got super close to finishing this, but the laser gave up at 9:55PM in heartbreaking fashion.

I started it up on Wednesday morning and laser cut it five times because I was super paranoid. I then laser cut the bottom and engraved it too. I'm skipping over some details here in that there were many rounds of iteration on illustrator files here that sucked.

There was a fun part where I actually used the Riemann sum to approximate the curve of my headphones and ported that to the curve of the case. Anyway, this was a total waste of tile because my measurements, even with the digital caliper and a jig, were probably not accurate. Or I messed up the math.

Anyway, my wooden pieces weren't the right size for the lid so I just had them as two slabs that I engraved and decided I'd glue together later.

For the jig I just used four pieces of wood to bend the acrylic against.

Eventually I had all the pieces together and what remained was the bending the sides across the jig and then cementing everything together.

The thinking for attaching the lid was to use a small, acrylic chip and a hole in the wood to hold a hinge screw with a spring.

Naturally, the first thing I did was snap my walls in half. Obviously an accident.

Anyway, I attempted to bend everything to the shape I desired anyway but couldn't quite get it.

I was too tired to actually get a photo of the final result--not exactly a looker--but here are some in process photos where the components look good. Sorry for not finishing the assignment again.
